subtitle: Planning a network graphics meeting for the early internet community.

tldr.problem: Project MAC at MIT wants to organize a dedicated meeting on network graphics, but first needs to gather input on what topics to cover.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 87 invites network sites to discuss graphics topics at an upcoming February working group meeting in Urbana, with plans for a larger dedicated graphics meeting in April.
tldr.outcome: The RFC coordinated planning among early network sites for specialized technical discussions.

today: RFC 87 is not Internet Standard. It documents early network community organizing. While dedicated graphics protocols did not emerge from these meetings, the approach of focused technical communities meeting to develop standards became a model that helped shape later internet culture.

sections.title: Planning the Graphics Meeting
sections.content:
A. Vezza of Project MAC at MIT proposes planning a network graphics meeting for April 1971. Before holding the full meeting, MIT wants to discuss it at the upcoming February Network Working Group meeting in Urbana to finalize the format, length and content.

Project MAC suggests the April meeting last two full days, with each organization presenting working papers on graphics topics they choose. The bulk of time would be prepared presentations with discussion afterwards, and the last few hours would be reserved for open discussion, critiques and planning.
sections.plainLanguage: We want to have a meeting about graphics on the network. What should we talk about?

sections.title: Proposed Content
sections.content:
The RFC outlines four content areas: descriptions of graphical facilities already connected to the network or planned to be, functional descriptions of graphical facilities one might envision or wish to see supported, proposals on network graphics protocols (even preliminary ones to discuss issues), and shared experiences with network graphics work, including problems encountered, solutions developed and insights gained.

Each participating organization is asked to prepare at least one working paper on one or more of these topics and present it at the April meeting, with authors determined by each organization.
sections.plainLanguage: Show what graphics systems you have or want. Suggest rules for sending graphics over the network. Tell war stories about what you tried.

sections.title: How to Participate
sections.content:
The RFC asks each organization to bring a list of its people actively engaged in graphics and related network work to the February meeting in Urbana. Suggestions for the April meeting agenda can be sent to Fran Yost or A. Vezza at Project MAC before the February meeting, by phone or mail to Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The RFC reflects the early network's culture of face-to-face working group meetings where technical communities self-organized around shared interests.
sections.plainLanguage: Send your ideas before February. Bring your people to Urbana to talk about it. We will figure out the April meeting from there.

sections.title: Scope
sections.content:
RFC 87 is a working document for organizing technical discussions within the early network community. It shows how research communities coordinated work across sites before formal standards organizations existed.

Network graphics was an early research frontier: remote access to graphics systems and protocols for transmitting visual information were not yet standardized. The proposed meeting would bring together researchers from different institutions to share work and identify common interests.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is basically a meeting invitation, showing how people organized technical work on the early network.
